Since Aparna joined last week, Usha has been following her everywhere. She holds Aparna's hand in the line, fetches her water, and tells me three times a day, "Aparna is SO nice, Ma'am! She's my best friend!" It's very loud. But I notice that when I praised Aparna's drawing today, Usha's smile stayed fixed and her hands squeezed together under the desk. Usha was the class's best drawer until last week. I think she may feel pushed aside and can't say it. What I did next: I asked Usha to help me put up the art wall, and I told her quietly that it's normal to feel a bit funny when someone new is good at the same thing. She stared at me, then nodded, very slowly.

qa.q: What was Usha known for until last week?
qa.a: Being the class's best drawer.

qa.q: What do Usha's fixed smile and squeezed hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Usha feels jealous and pushed aside, hiding it behind loud friendliness towards Aparna.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's quiet comment a good step?
qa.a: It told Usha that her feeling is normal without accusing her, making it easier to admit.

qa.q: How might Aparna see Usha's attention?
qa.a: Aparna may feel welcomed but perhaps a little overwhelmed by being followed everywhere.

grounding: Shows a child who feels displaced by a new classmate becoming overly sweet and clingy, the loud friendliness masking jealousy.

subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]
passage:
Dear diary, Rehana here.

Shreya is the new girl and she sits with Farah now. Farah was MY bench-partner since class one.

I gave Shreya my favourite strawberry eraser today. And my lunch. And I told everyone she's the nicest girl in the whole school, like five times. I even waited for her outside the washroom.

Mummy said, "Wah, you've made a new friend!" and I said yes, she's my best friend now.

But when Farah and Shreya laughed together in maths, my throat went tight, and I pressed my pencil so hard the tip broke.

I'm not jealous. I'm being NICE. Nice people aren't jealous.

Maybe I'll give Shreya my sticker book tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Rehana give Shreya today?
qa.a: The favourite strawberry eraser, and lunch.

qa.q: What do the tight throat and broken pencil tip reveal?
qa.a: They suggest Rehana feels jealous and hurt about losing Farah as a bench-partner, feelings hidden under all the niceness.

qa.q: How could a grown-up help Rehana with these feelings?
qa.a: Someone like Mummy could gently say that missing a friend and feeling jealous is normal, so Rehana doesn't have to prove it away with gifts.

qa.q: How might Farah feel about all the attention Rehana gives Shreya?
qa.a: Farah may feel confused, or even miss Rehana, not knowing the kindness hides hurt.

grounding: Shows a child who feels displaced by a new classmate becoming overly generous and clingy, masking jealousy they cannot admit.

subtype: Mocking the one who is liked [Actor]
passage: In the Bengaluru school corridor, Tenzin's friends were sitting on the steps when Nitin walked past with his guitar case. "Oh look, it's the rock star," Tenzin called loudly. "Going to sing your sad songs to the canteen?" Her friends laughed. Nitin went red and kept walking. Tenzin laughed too, louder than anyone. But her cheeks were burning. She'd listened to him play at the school fest last month and hadn't been able to stop thinking about it. She'd rather die than let anyone know. Teasing was safe. Nobody teases someone they like, everyone knows that. That evening, at home, she found herself scrolling back through the fest videos, pausing on the one where he looked up and smiled. She felt a little sick about the canteen joke.

qa.q: What was Nitin carrying when he walked past?
qa.a: His guitar case.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin tease Nitin so loudly?
qa.a: She had a crush on him and felt terrified of anyone finding out, so mocking him loudly protected her from feeling exposed.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do tomorrow to make things better?
qa.a: She could say a simple, genuine thing, like that she liked his playing at the fest, or at least stop the teasing.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel after being called the rock star in front of everyone?
qa.a: Nitin likely felt embarrassed and hurt, with no idea that the teasing hid a crush.

passage:
"Mohit, your handwriting is SO bad. Did a chicken write this?"
The group round Kashish's desk laughed.
"Very funny, Kashish."
"And why do you always wear that same blue jacket? Don't you own anything else?"
More laughter. Mohit shrugged and went back to his seat.
Anjali leaned over. "Why are you always on his case?"
"Because he's annoying."
"He's not, though."
"He is! Everything about him is annoying." Kashish's face was hot.
Anjali narrowed her eyes. "Wait. Do you like him?"
"Eww! No! Are you mad?"
"You've talked about his jacket three times this week."
"Because it's ugly!"
Kashish stared at her book, heart pounding, and did not look at the blue jacket for the rest of the period.

qa.a: She could simply be friendly or stay neutral, which is less hurtful to Mohit even if she isn't ready to share her feelings.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel about Kashish's comments?
qa.a: Mohit probably feels puzzled and a little hurt, picked on for his handwriting and jacket without knowing why.

subtype: Mocking the one who is liked [Actor]
passage: I'm Tejas. In class ten there was a girl in my tuition batch, Meher, and I spent the whole year making fun of her in front of everyone. Her laugh, her giant water bottle, the way she asked too many questions. My friend Nitin finally cornered me at the tea stall. "Every day it's Meher this, Meher that. You're obsessed." I said something like, "Obsessed with how weird she is." He just looked at me. And I felt my face burn, because he'd seen it before I had. I liked her. I'd liked her since the first week. Teasing her loudly was my way of making sure nobody, including me, could guess. I didn't do anything brave after that. But I stopped the jokes. And once, near the end of the year, I told her I liked her questions. She smiled.

qa.q: Who cornered the narrator at the tea stall?
qa.a: Nitin.

qa.q: Why did Tejas's face burn when Nitin just looked?
qa.a: Tejas felt exposed and embarrassed, because Nitin had seen the crush behind the teasing before Tejas had admitted it.

qa.q: What small steps did Tejas take once the truth came out?
qa.a: Stopping the jokes and later telling Meher something kind and true about her questions.

qa.q: How might Meher have felt when told her questions were liked?
qa.a: Meher probably felt surprised and pleased, after a year of being mocked for the same thing.

grounding: Shows a teenager with a crush teasing the person loudly in front of friends, the opposite behaviour protecting them from feeling exposed.

passage: In the village near Sirsa, the whole family talked about Chaitanya, who had left the farm to join a travelling folk-theatre group. Manoj talked the loudest. "Dancing in a painted face for strangers! Shameful. A grown man. Our grandfather would be ashamed." He said it at dinner, at the well, at the tea shop. His uncle raised an eyebrow. "You've said that four times today, Manoj." But in the evenings, when the tractor was in the shed and nobody was around, Manoj would hum the old Haryanvi songs Chaitanya used to sing and, very quietly, try the steps in the dust behind the cowshed. Once his little cousin caught him. Manoj shouted at her to go inside. Then he stood there, breathing hard, not sure who he was angriest at.

qa.q: What group did Chaitanya join?
qa.a: A travelling folk-theatre group.

qa.q: Why does Manoj condemn Chaitanya so often and so loudly?
qa.a: The unusual heat suggests Manoj is secretly drawn to singing and dancing himself, and scorning Chaitanya helps him push down that tempting, shameful wish.

qa.q: What might help Manoj with the feeling underneath?
qa.a: Admitting to himself, or a trusted person, that he loves the songs and steps, instead of fighting it by attacking Chaitanya.

qa.q: How might Manoj's little cousin see what happened behind the cowshed?
qa.a: She might be confused and scared, catching him dancing and then being shouted at for it.

subtype: Fierce scorn for a secret temptation [Actor]
passage: In a café in Lisbon, Clara was mid-rant again. "Gap years are just rich kids being lazy. Six months on a beach finding yourself? Please. Real adults work." Santiago stirred his coffee. "You've said that about three times this week." "Because it's true." "Your cousin's doing one. You got very angry at her Christmas card." "Because it was smug." Santiago tilted his head. "Clara. I saw your laptop yesterday. You had eleven tabs open about volunteering in Chile." Clara went pink. "That was research. For an argument." "An argument with who?" She opened her mouth, closed it, and looked at the window. Outside, a tram went past with an advert for cheap flights. She watched it all the way down the street.

qa.q: How many tabs did Clara have open about volunteering in Chile?
qa.a: Eleven tabs.

qa.q: Why did Clara go pink when Santiago mentioned her laptop?
qa.a: Clara felt embarrassed and exposed, because her fierce scorn for gap years hid her own longing to go.

qa.q: What could Clara do next with that longing?
qa.a: She could look honestly at whether a volunteering trip is something she wants, instead of attacking others for wanting it.

qa.q: How does Santiago read Clara's rants?
qa.a: Santiago suspects that the heat means the opposite feeling, noticing the repeated rants and the Chile tabs.

subtype: Over-the-top praise from a rival [Observer]
passage: At the Chennai bank's regional office, the promotion to branch manager went to Nandan. Everyone clapped. But Lokesh noticed Trisha, who had also applied, clapping longest and loudest. At lunch she said, "Nandan is honestly the best choice. He's brilliant. I'm so happy for him." Twice at tea she said it again, almost word for word. She sent a long congratulations message to the whole team, full of exclamation marks. Lokesh didn't think she was faking, exactly. But the praise was a bit too much, too often. He remembered how many late evenings she'd put in on her application. It seemed more like someone trying to settle a sting than someone plotting. So he didn't gossip. At the end of the day he just said to her, "You had a strong application too. That must be hard." Trisha's smile wavered. "It is, a bit," she said.

qa.q: Who got the promotion to branch manager?
qa.a: Nandan.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh think Trisha's praise was a sign of mixed feelings rather than ill will?
qa.a: Lokesh felt thoughtful and sympathetic, noticing the praise was excessive and repeated, and knowing how hard she had worked, so it looked like disappointment rather than scheming.

qa.q: Why was Lokesh's quiet comment wise?
qa.a: It gently acknowledged her disappointment without accusing her, giving her room to admit her feelings.

qa.q: What might Trisha feel when her smile wavers?
qa.a: Trisha likely feels disappointed and a little relieved to have someone notice how hard it is.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a rival gushing about a promotion too much and too often, and reading it as mixed feelings rather than ill will.

subtype: Over-the-top praise from a rival [Observer]
passage:
Ganga,

Something odd since my promotion. Farzana, who applied for the same role, has congratulated me every single day this week. Monday: a card. Tuesday: a speech at the team huddle about how I'm "the most deserving person in this entire building." Wednesday: a cake. Thursday: she told my manager, in front of me, that I'm a genius. It's a lot.

My first thought was that she's secretly furious and planning something. But I don't think that's fair. Nobody has done anything unkind. I think she's disappointed and doesn't want to look disappointed, so it's coming out as extra praise.

So I'm not going to be suspicious. I'm going to ask her for coffee and ask about the project she wants to lead next.

What do you think?

Ishita

qa.q: What did Farzana bring on Wednesday?
qa.a: A cake.

qa.q: Why did Ishita decide not to treat Farzana's praise as a plot?
qa.a: Ishita felt wary at first but then fair-minded, seeing that nobody had done anything unkind and that the extra praise more likely hid Farzana's disappointment.

qa.q: What makes Ishita's coffee plan a good idea?
qa.a: It shows respect for Farzana's ambitions and opens a real conversation, instead of treating her as a threat.

qa.q: How might Farzana be feeling underneath all the congratulations?
qa.a: Farzana may feel disappointed and a little embarrassed, and eager not to look bitter.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a rival gushing about Ishita's promotion too often, and reading the excess as mixed feelings rather than proof of ill will.

subtype: Over-the-top praise from a rival [Observer]
passage: Deepak, you asked why I've been watching Harish so closely. Here's the thing, from me, Chinmay. When Anu got the team lead role, Harish, who'd wanted it badly, stood up in the meeting and gave a five-minute speech about how she was the perfect choice. Then he posted about it on the office board. Then he told the client she was "a once-in-a-generation talent." Every day, something new. At first I thought, he's being sarcastic, or he's setting her up. But I looked at him properly. He wasn't smirking. He looked tired. I think the praise is how he's handling the disappointment, trying to be the bigger person a bit too loudly. It's a clue that he's got mixed feelings. It's not proof that he wants her to fail. So I've stopped watching him for sabotage. I asked him to lunch instead.

qa.a: "A once-in-a-generation talent."

qa.a: Looking closer, Chinmay saw that Harish looked tired, not smug, and felt more sympathy than suspicion, reading the praise as mixed feelings.

qa.a: Chinmay could ask how Harish is doing and what he hopes for next, making room for his disappointment without accusing him.
